2023 · ICLR 2024 · Agents

SOTOPIA: Interactive Evaluation for Social Intelligence in Language Agents

Give two LLM agents a private social goal each — keep the blanket, get the blanket back — drop them into one of 90 scripted scenarios played out by 40 procedurally-generated characters, and score the transcript on seven axes instead of one. SOTOPIA turns social intelligence from a static QA benchmark into an interactive, goal-driven simulation, then asks whether GPT-4 itself can be trusted to referee it.

Xuhui Zhou, Hao Zhu, Leena Mathur, Ruohong Zhang, Zhengyang Qi, Haofei Yu, Louis-Philippe Morency, Yonatan Bisk, Daniel Fried, Graham Neubig, Maarten Sap

// the gap

What problem is this solving?

Social intelligence — balancing a goal against a friend's need for personal space, a stranger's secret, a bargaining partner's bottom line — is exactly the kind of multi-motive, interactive skill that a single-turn QA benchmark can't capture. Yet nearly every existing social-intelligence benchmark is single-turn QA: ToMi and FauxPas probe theory-of-mind with reading-comprehension questions, SocialIQA and Social-IQ score multiple-choice answers about a static vignette or video clip. None of them make an agent actually act under conflicting incentives and then live with the consequences. The interactive alternatives that do exist cut the other way — they're narrow. PersonaChat and its descendants are open-ended chit-chat with no explicit goal to fail at; Deal-or-No-Deal, CraigslistBargain and TEACh each cover one task type (negotiation, or embodied instruction-following) rather than a broad space of social situations; and simulation work like Generative Agents (Park et al., 2023) shows LLM characters can look believable in a Sims-style sandbox, but never scores them against an explicit, multi-dimensional rubric — believability was the whole point, not one axis among several. What's missing is an environment that is simultaneously interactive (agents act, observe, and adapt across turns), open-ended (scenarios, characters and relationships are generated procedurally rather than hand-authored one at a time), and evaluated on the full mix of human motives — goal completion, but also relationship maintenance, financial stakes, information gained, secrets kept, and social norms followed or broken — because real people rarely optimize just one of those at a time.

// how it works

The method

SOTOPIA builds a large combinatorial task space out of three GPT-4-generated, human-validated axes: 90 scenarios (shared context plus a private social goal per side — e.g. "sell an antique chair, buyer wants it for $80, seller wants $90"), 40 characters (name, occupation, personality traits, moral and Schwartz values, decision-making style, plus a secret and public backstory), and 5 relationship types (family, friend, romantic, acquaintance, stranger) that both constrain which characters can be paired for a scenario and gate how much of each other's profile they can see — strangers see nothing, acquaintances see name/occupation/public info, family/friends/romantic partners see everything except secrets. Sampling 5 character pairs per scenario yields 450 tasks. In an episode, two agents take turns (round-robin, 20-turn cap) choosing one of five action types — speak, non-verbal communication, physical action, none, or leave — each realized as free text (e.g. speak("Hello Bob!")). Formally this is an N-agent Dec-POMDP with a vector-valued reward: instead of one scalar, each agent gets scored post-hoc along seven dimensions that make up SOTOPIA-EVAL: Goal Completion (GOAL), Believability (BEL), Knowledge (KNO), Relationship (REL), Financial/Material benefits (FIN), Social Rules (SOC), and Secret-keeping (SEC) — each on its own bounded scale (see the equation below), scored by GPT-4 or humans reading the full transcript with the same rubric.

R(ai) = ⟨ rGOAL, rBEL, rKNO, rREL, rFIN, rSOC, rSEC ⟩ // SOTOPIA-EVAL's reward is 7-dimensional, not a single scalar. GOAL/BEL/KNO ∈ [0,10], REL/FIN ∈ [-5,5], SOC/SEC ∈ [-10,0] (only negative — keeping secrets and following norms is the baseline expectation, not a bonus)

The 90 scenarios and 40 characters are themselves LLM-generated: GPT-4 is prompted with seed examples pulled from prior social datasets (SocialIQA, Deal-or-No-Deal, NormBank, CraigslistBargain) to "inspire" new scenario text, the authors manually validate and prune roughly 10% of the output, and the same GPT-4-authoring pattern produces character profiles and plausible relationships between them. The paper simulates 450 tasks across four models (GPT-4-0613, GPT-3.5-turbo-16k-0613, Llama-2-70b-chat, MPT-30b-chat, enumerated as all model×model pairs) plus a separate human-in-the-loop study on a curated hard subset.

// what they found

The results

Averaged across all partner-model pairings, GPT-4 leads every SOTOPIA-EVAL dimension: GOAL 7.62 vs. GPT-3.5's 6.45, Llama-2-70b-chat's 5.38, and MPT-30b-chat's 4.10 (all differences significant at p<0.05); the same ordering holds for REL (1.94 vs. 1.23 / 0.91 / 0.58), FIN (0.81 vs. 0.46 / 0.40 / 0.28), and BEL (9.28 vs. 9.15 / 8.10 / 6.17). But the ranking inverts a well-known static-benchmark result: Llama-2-70b-chat is reported as on par with or better than GPT-3.5 on MMLU-style leaderboards, yet it trails GPT-3.5 on almost every SOTOPIA dimension — the authors' hypothesis is that Llama-2 is less heavily RLHF'd on multi-turn human interaction than GPT-3.5. A pairwise heatmap (Figure 3, bottom) shows a second effect: a weak partner drags its counterpart down too — GPT-4 paired with GPT-4 averages 3.32 overall, but GPT-4 paired with MPT-30b-chat drops to 1.76, and inspecting transcripts shows MPT/Llama-2 repeatedly failing to maintain persona or respond to what the other agent just said. No model comes out clean on the norm-following axes: SOC and SEC are negative for all four models (e.g. GPT-4 SOC −0.07, SEC −0.14), meaning even the best model still leaks secrets and breaks social rules on average.

A separate human-vs-model study narrows to SOTOPIA-hard — the 20 scenarios where the gap between the best-case and worst-case reward (mean ± 3σ) is largest for GPT-4 — and runs 40 human–GPT-4 and 20 human–human interactions there. Humans playing against GPT-4 hit GOAL 5.95 and humans playing each other hit 6.15, both significantly higher than GPT-4 playing against humans at 4.85 (p<0.05); every other dimension is statistically indistinguishable. Humans are also far more concise — 16.8 words per turn versus GPT-4's 45.5 — and more strategic: in bargaining transcripts GPT-4 sometimes opens right at its target price (leaving no room to negotiate up, so any further haggling only pushes the price past that target), while human negotiators open lower — e.g. $400 against a $454 target — and often close the deal below GPT-4's target, the better outcome.

// does it hold up?

The eval read

The paper's central empirical claim — that GPT-4 can stand in for human judgment — is tested honestly: 200 episodes are double-scored by pre-qualified Mechanical Turk workers and by GPT-4 on the same 11-point rubric, and the paper reports the correlation is uneven rather than uniformly strong. Table 1's Pearson correlations are highest on GOAL (0.71 when models role-play, 0.78 when humans do) and lowest on SEC (0.22) and KNO (0.19–0.33); more than 74% of GPT-4 scores land within one human standard deviation of the human mean, but the residual is skewed — GPT-4 disagrees upward far more often than downward (Figure 2), and Appendix G.3 shows it specifically over-rates SOC and SEC relative to humans, i.e. it's most miscalibrated on exactly the dimensions (norm-following, secret-keeping) where the headline Table 2 result — "all models leak secrets and break rules" — depends on trusting the automated grader. The paper is upfront about this ("one should be aware of the influence of these potential biases") but doesn't quantify how much of the SOC/SEC gap across models is genuine behavior versus grader miscalibration in the same direction for every model.

The structural issue underneath all of this is that GPT-4 is not an independent judge: it authors the scenarios and characters agents role-play in (via the generation prompts in §2.1), it is itself one of the four models being compared, and it is the evaluator scoring Table 2's automated results (footnote 9 notes the human-eval trend is "similar," reported only in an appendix, not as the headline number). A self-preference effect in LLM-as-judge setups is well documented elsewhere in the literature the paper itself cites (Wang et al., 2023, "LLMs are not Fair Evaluators"), and SOTOPIA's design doesn't rule it out for its own headline GPT-4-vs-others ranking. Human inter-annotator agreement is also only "moderate" (Randolph's κ = 0.503), which sets a real noise floor against which the reported model deltas (e.g. GOAL 7.62 vs. 6.45) should be read — the gap between GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 is not enormous relative to how much two human raters can already disagree.

baselines

GPT-4-0613, GPT-3.5-turbo-16k-0613, Llama-2-70b-chat, MPT-30b-chat — a reasonable spread for late 2023 but already stale a year later: no Claude, no Llama-3/4, no post-training methods designed for social interaction, and none of the frontier 2025-era reasoning models.

contamination

Scenarios and characters are GPT-4-generated (with human validation and ~10% pruning) but seeded from prior public datasets — SocialIQA, Deal-or-No-Deal, NormBank, CraigslistBargain — that GPT-4 likely saw in pretraining; the sharper conflict is structural rather than textual: the same model family authors the scenario, plays one of the two roles, and (in the automated Table 2 numbers) grades the transcript.

what's missed

Human inter-rater agreement is only "moderate" (κ=0.503), so part of every reported model delta could be scorer noise; GPT-4-as-judge is most miscalibrated exactly on SOC/SEC, the dimensions driving the "every model leaks secrets" finding; the "creative solution" anecdotes (§6) are illustrative examples, never a measured frequency; and the 20-turn cap can truncate the very multi-step negotiations SOTOPIA is designed to probe.

would raise confidence

A judge model independent of the model family being evaluated corroborating Table 2's ranking; per-dimension (not just pooled) human-agreement statistics; an explicit novelty/decontamination check against the seed datasets; and a rerun with current-generation models now that GPT-4-0613 and MPT-30b-chat are two-plus generations behind the frontier.

// bottom line

SOTOPIA is a genuine design advance — interactive, goal-driven, multi-dimensional, where prior social-intelligence evals were static QA — and its human-agreement study is a real, if partial, validation of automated scoring. But the same model (GPT-4) writes the scenario, plays a role in it, and grades the outcome, and the paper's own numbers show that model over-rating exactly the dimensions its headline claims depend on. Read SOTOPIA-EVAL scores as directional signal about relative model behavior, corroborated by a modest human study, not as a calibrated absolute scale.

// takeaways

What to remember

  1. SOTOPIA replaces static social-intelligence QA with an interactive, goal-driven simulation over a combinatorial task space — 90 scenarios × 40 characters × 5 relationship types, sampled into 450 tasks — scored on seven dimensions (GOAL, BEL, KNO, REL, FIN, SOC, SEC) instead of one accuracy number.
  2. GPT-4 tracks human judgment well enough to serve as an automatic grader on GOAL, FIN and REL (Pearson r up to 0.71/0.62/0.56, >74% of scores within one human standard deviation), but it is simultaneously the scenario author, one of the four models being graded, and the grader — and it over-rates itself relative to humans exactly on the SOC/SEC axes its "every model breaks rules" finding depends on.
  3. Model rankings on SOTOPIA don't reproduce static-benchmark rankings — Llama-2-70b-chat, competitive with GPT-3.5 on conventional leaderboards, trails it on nearly every SOTOPIA-EVAL dimension — and every model, GPT-4 included, still averages negative SOC/SEC scores and loses to humans on the 20 hardest scenarios (SOTOPIA-hard GOAL: 4.85 for GPT-4 vs. 5.95–6.15 for humans).
